triage.name: Tendinitis
triage.reason: Common overuse injury with focal pain and exam findings; straightforward diagnosis with good differential teaching.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'x-ray of the affected region' was in ['supporting', 'not_indicated'], kept ['not_indicated', 'supporting']

auto-repaired: workup: 'X-ray of the affected region' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if trauma, focal bony tenderness, or another bony cause is suspected)
presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common in people who do repetitive or forceful activities with the affected limb
Slightly more common in males for sport-related tendinitis
Common in working-age adults with physically demanding jobs

risk_factors.text: Repetitive or forceful use of the affected tendon (sports, manual labor, keyboarding)
Sudden increase in training intensity, duration, or frequency
Poor technique or improper equipment (e.g., racquet grip, running shoes)

social_history: Participation in racket sports, throwing sports, running, or swimming
Occupations involving repetitive gripping, lifting, or overhead work

chief_complaints.text: My elbow hurts when I use it
It hurts right here where the tendon attaches
The pain started after I increased my activity

hpi.onset: Gradual, over days to weeks, often after a change in activity or repetitive use
hpi.duration: Usually weeks to months at presentation
hpi.progression: Pain starts mild and activity-related, then becomes more frequent and can occur with light activity or at rest if untreated
hpi.location: Focal, directly over the affected tendon near its attachment to bone (e.g., lateral elbow, shoulder, wrist, Achilles, patellar tendon)
hpi.radiation: Usually none; may spread a few centimeters along the tendon
hpi.quality: Aching, sore, or burning; sometimes sharp with specific movements
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate, typically 3–6/10; worse with activity
hpi.timing: Worse with activity and at the start of movement; may ease after warm-up, then ache afterward
aggravating: Repetitive or forceful use of the affected limb

associated_symptoms.text: Mild swelling or thickening over the tendon
Stiffness in the morning or after inactivity
Weakness or feeling that the limb gives way with use
A grating or creaking sensation with movement

pertinent_negatives: Redness, warmth, or spreading skin infection over the joint
Locking, catching, or true giving-way of the joint
Numbness, tingling, or weakness in a nerve distribution
Pain and stiffness in many joints or symmetric small joints
Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Recent significant trauma or a fall
Night pain that wakes them from sleep
Weight loss, night sweats, or malaise

positives.text: Focal pain over a tendon with use
Tenderness to touch over the tendon
Mild swelling or thickening of the tendon

negatives: Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour

atypical.how_it_differs: Pain may be more chronic and attributed to arthritis; degenerative tendon changes are common and symptoms can be less clearly tied to a single activity.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal link to a new activity

atypical.how_it_differs: Tendon healing is impaired and tendinitis can be more persistent and recurrent, sometimes with less dramatic pain.
Increased load on weight-bearing tendons (Achilles, patellar) can cause more gradual, less activity-specific pain.
Overuse tendinitis is less common; apophysitis (e.g., Osgood-Schlatter, Sever disease) is more likely and pain localizes to the growth plate rather than the tendon.
missing_classic_features: Tenderness directly over the tendon midsubstance

general.mild: Comfortable at rest, no distress; moves the limb normally until the tendon is loaded
general.moderate: Guards the affected limb with use, mild discomfort on active movement
general.severe: Visibly uncomfortable with any active use of the limb, avoids the aggravating motion
general.critical: Not applicable; tendinitis does not cause a toxic or systemically ill appearance

findings.maneuver: Palpate along the course of the affected tendon, especially near its bony attachment
findings.finding: Focal tenderness directly over the tendon, maximal at the insertion or midsubstance

findings.maneuver: Have the patient actively contract the affected muscle against resistance while isolating that tendon
findings.finding: Reproduction of the patient's pain at the tendon with resisted contraction

findings.maneuver: Passively stretch the musculotendinous unit across the joint it crosses
findings.finding: Pain localized to the tendon with passive stretch

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the tendon for enlargement compared with the contralateral side
findings.finding: Mild fusiform swelling or thickening of the tendon

findings.maneuver: Move the affected joint through its range while palpating the tendon
findings.finding: A grating or creaking sensation over the tendon

findings.maneuver: Test strength of the affected muscle group against resistance
findings.finding: Mildly reduced power limited by pain, with full strength when pain is overcome

findings.maneuver: Inspect and ballotte the adjacent joint for fluid
findings.finding: No joint effusion or synovial swelling

findings.maneuver: Stress the joint and assess for giving-way or laxity
findings.finding: No ligamentous laxity or true instability

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin over the tendon for erythema, warmth, and drainage
findings.finding: No redness, warmth, or open wound over the tendon

findings.maneuver: Test sensation and strength in the distribution of the nerves crossing the region
findings.finding: No sensory loss or weakness in a nerve distribution

findings.maneuver: Assess for fever, rash, and generalized joint involvement
findings.finding: No fever, rash, or polyarticular involvement

imaging.preferred_when: First-line when the diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms are persistent

findings.text: Tendon thickening and hypoechoic swelling of the tendon substance
Increased intrasubstance signal with loss of the normal fibrillar pattern
Peritendinous fluid or increased Doppler flow (hyperemia) around the tendon
Normal-appearing tendon (does not exclude clinical tendinitis)

imaging.preferred_when: Persistent symptoms, suspected partial or full-thickness tear, or when ultrasound is nondiagnostic

findings.text: Tendon thickening with increased T2 signal within the tendon substance
Peritendinous edema and soft tissue inflammation
Degenerative intrasubstance changes without discrete tear

imaging.preferred_when: Only when fracture, dislocation, or another bony cause is suspected

findings.text: Normal bone and joint (typical in tendinitis)
Tendon calcification or enthesophyte at the tendon insertion
Degenerative joint changes if coexisting arthritis

initial.why: Confirms tendon swelling or tear and excludes other causes when the diagnosis is uncertain
initial.only_if: diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms are persistent despite rest

confirmatory.why: Most accurate for characterizing tendon degeneration, partial tears, and excluding other soft tissue causes
confirmatory.only_if: symptoms persist, a tear is suspected, or ultrasound is nondiagnostic

supporting.why: Excludes fracture, dislocation, or bony abnormality
supporting.only_if: trauma, focal bony tenderness, or another bony cause is suspected

not_indicated.why: No role in a focal overuse tendon injury without fever or systemic signs
Not needed unless inflammatory arthritis or infection is suspected
Not needed unless inflammatory arthritis or polymyalgia rheumatica is suspected
Not indicated unless myositis or muscle injury is suspected
Not indicated unless gout is suspected

decision_points: Tendinitis is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is reserved for uncertain, persistent, or atypical cases
Ultrasound is the first-line imaging study when imaging is needed
MRI is reserved for suspected tear or when ultrasound is nondiagnostic
X-ray only if fracture, dislocation, or bony pathology is suspected

differential.name: Rotator cuff tear
differential.why_considered: Shoulder pain with overhead activity and weakness, often attributed to tendinitis
differential.trigger: Weakness that is out of proportion to pain, or a history of a pop with acute injury

history: Sudden onset after a fall, lift, or pull, or a pop felt at the time of injury
Weakness with overhead reaching or lifting that persists even when pain is controlled
Inability to lift the arm against gravity
exam: Marked weakness on resisted abduction or external rotation that does not improve when pain is relieved
Positive empty can or external rotation lag sign
imaging: Full-thickness or high-grade partial-thickness tear on ultrasound or MRI
Tendon retraction or muscle atrophy on MRI

differential.name: Septic tenosynovitis or septic arthritis
differential.why_considered: Painful, swollen tendon or joint region that can be mistaken for inflammatory tendinitis
differential.trigger: Fever, marked focal warmth and redness, or inability to move the digit or joint at all

history: Fever and chills
Rapid onset over hours to a day
Recent penetrating injury, bite, or immunosuppression
exam: Erythema, warmth, and severe tenderness along the tendon sheath
Pain with passive extension of the digit (Kanavel signs in flexor tenosynovitis)
labs: Positive blood cultures or purulent aspirate with organisms on Gram stain
imaging: Ultrasound showing fluid distending the tendon sheath
MRI showing sheath fluid and surrounding soft tissue edema

differential.name: Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis or spondyloarthritis)
differential.why_considered: Joint and periarticular pain with swelling that can be attributed to tendinitis

history: Symmetric small joint involvement
Morning stiffness lasting more than an hour
Constitutional symptoms such as fatigue and weight loss
exam: Involvement of multiple joints rather than a single tendon
Extra-articular findings such as nodules or rash
imaging: Erosions and symmetric joint space narrowing on X-ray
Synovitis and bone marrow edema on MRI

differential.name: Gout or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease
differential.why_considered: Acute focal pain and swelling near a joint or tendon insertion

history: Sudden severe onset, often overnight
Prior similar attacks
History of kidney stones or diuretic use
exam: Intensely red, warm, exquisitely tender joint
labs: Elevated serum uric acid (may be normal during an attack)
Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals on joint aspirate
imaging: Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges on X-ray

differential.name: Nerve entrapment (carpal tunnel syndrome or radial tunnel syndrome)
differential.why_considered: Wrist or forearm pain with activity that can mimic wrist extensor or flexor tendinitis

history: Numbness and tingling in a nerve distribution
Nighttime symptoms that wake the patient
Symptoms provoked by sustained wrist flexion or extension
exam: Sensory loss in the median or radial nerve distribution
Weakness of thenar muscles in advanced carpal tunnel syndrome
labs: Nerve conduction studies showing focal slowing
imaging: Ultrasound showing enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area

differential.name: Stress fracture
differential.why_considered: Activity-related focal pain in a weight-bearing or repetitive-load region

history: Pain that is worse with weight-bearing and improves with rest
Recent increase in running or marching distance
Pain that progresses to occur at rest or at night
exam: Focal bony tenderness rather than tendon tenderness
Pain with axial loading or hopping on the affected leg
imaging: Periosteal reaction or fracture line on X-ray (may be normal early)
Bone marrow edema or fracture line on MRI

differential.name: Polymyalgia rheumatica
differential.why_considered: Shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness in older adults

history: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness
Morning stiffness lasting more than 45 minutes
Age over 50
exam: Pain with active range of motion but preserved passive range of motion

severity.mild: Pain only with the aggravating activity, no pain at rest, no swelling, full strength, and full range of motion
severity.moderate: Pain with light activity and at the start of movement, mild swelling or thickening over the tendon, stiffness after rest, and mildly reduced power limited by pain
severity.severe: Pain at rest or with any use of the limb, marked tenderness and swelling, and significant functional limitation that interferes with work or daily activities
severity.critical: Not applicable; tendinitis is not life-threatening, but a suspected tendon rupture or septic tenosynovitis requires urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Sudden pop with immediate loss of strength or inability to move the limb
red_flags.meaning: Tendon rupture; needs urgent orthopedic evaluation

red_flags.finding: Fever, chills, or marked focal warmth and redness over the tendon
red_flags.meaning: Septic tenosynovitis or septic arthritis; needs aspiration and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Inability to bear weight or use the limb at all after trauma
Numbness, tingling, or weakness in a nerve distribution
red_flags.meaning: Nerve entrapment or radiculopathy rather than isolated tendinitis

red_flags.finding: Night pain that wakes the patient from sleep or unexplained weight loss
Pain and stiffness in multiple joints with morning stiffness over an hour

complications.name: Chronic tendinopathy
clues: Symptoms persisting beyond 6 to 12 weeks despite rest

complications.name: Partial-thickness tendon tear
clues: Increase in pain with a specific movement
Intrasubstance tear on ultrasound or MRI

complications.name: Full-thickness tendon rupture
clues: Inability to perform the tendon's action against resistance

complications.name: Reduced work or sports participation
clues: Decreased grip strength or throwing velocity
Limitation in overhead reaching or running

special_populations.differences: Degenerative tendon changes are common, symptoms may be more chronic and less clearly linked to a single activity, and the differential includes polymyalgia rheumatica and rotator cuff tear.
Tendon healing is impaired, tendinitis is more persistent and recurrent, and the risk of tendon rupture is higher.
Increased load on weight-bearing tendons such as the Achilles and patellar tendons leads to more gradual, less activity-specific pain.
Overuse tendinitis is less common; apophysitis such as Osgood-Schlatter disease or Sever disease is more likely, with tenderness over the growth plate rather than the tendon midsubstance.

key_questions.question: Where exactly is the pain, and can you point to it with one finger?
key_questions.looking_for: Focal pain directly over a tendon near its bony attachment (lateral elbow, shoulder, wrist, Achilles, patellar tendon)

key_questions.question: Did the pain start suddenly after an injury, or build up gradually?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over days to weeks; sudden onset with a pop suggests a tear

key_questions.question: Did anything change in your activity before this started, such as a new sport, more training, or more repetitive work?
key_questions.looking_for: A recent increase in repetitive or forceful use of the affected limb

key_questions.question: What movements make it worse, and what makes it better?
key_questions.looking_for: Worse with resisted use of the tendon, gripping, lifting, or overhead reaching; better with rest and ice

key_questions.question: Does the pain ease after you warm up, then ache afterward?
Is there any swelling, stiffness, or a grating feeling over the tendon?
key_questions.looking_for: Mild focal swelling or thickening, morning stiffness, or crepitus

key_questions.question: Do you feel weak or like the limb gives way when you use it?
key_questions.looking_for: Weakness limited by pain; true giving-way or persistent weakness suggests a tear

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills, or redness and warmth over the area?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests septic tenosynovitis or septic arthritis

key_questions.question: Did you feel a sudden pop with immediate loss of strength or inability to move the limb?
Do you have pain or stiffness in many joints, especially in the morning?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; symmetric small joint pain with morning stiffness over an hour suggests inflammatory arthritis

key_questions.question: Have you taken antibiotics in the last few months, especially a fluoroquinolone?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, or moxifloxacin use, which raises tendon injury risk

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes or another chronic illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes or inflammatory arthritis, which affect tendon healing and the differential

key_questions.question: What sports or work activities do you do that involve repetitive gripping, lifting, or overhead motion?
key_questions.looking_for: Racket sports, throwing sports, running, swimming, or manual labor with repetitive use

key_questions.question: Any numbness, tingling, or weakness in a nerve distribution?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests nerve entrapment or radiculopathy

key_questions.question: Does the pain wake you from sleep, or have you had unexplained weight loss or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present raises concern for infection or malignancy

reasoning_points: Focal pain directly over a tendon near its bony attachment
Gradual onset after a recent increase in repetitive or forceful activity
Pain reproduced by resisted contraction and passive stretch of the affected musculotendinous unit
Mild focal tendon swelling or thickening without joint effusion
No fever, erythema, or systemic signs to suggest infection
No true instability, locking, or nerve deficit
Imaging reserved for uncertain, persistent, or atypical cases

easy: Classic activity-related focal tendon pain in a young or middle-aged adult
Clear temporal link to a new or increased activity
Focal tenderness over the tendon with pain on resisted contraction
No joint effusion, fever, or systemic symptoms
medium: Older adult with degenerative tendon changes and less clear activity trigger
Pain that overlaps with a joint or bursa, making the source less obvious
Mild swelling and stiffness that raise concern for inflammatory arthritis
Coexisting diabetes with more persistent symptoms
hard: Sudden pop with weakness suggesting a partial or full-thickness tear
Fever and focal warmth suggesting septic tenosynovitis
Numbness and tingling suggesting nerve entrapment rather than tendinitis
Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain in an older adult suggesting polymyalgia rheumatica
Activity-related focal pain that is actually a stress fracture
